BEFORE THE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
                       OF THE STATE OF MISSOURI
In the Matter of Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a )
Evergy Missouri Metro’s Request for       ) File No. ER-2026-0143
Authority to Implement a General Rate     )
Increase for Electric Service             )

     Velvet Tech Services, LLC’s Initial Post-Hearing Brief

     Velvet Tech Services, LLC (“Velvet”) submits this brief on the issues
affecting customers taking service under the Large Load Power Service
(“LLPS”) tariff of Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro (“Evergy”).
Velvet’s position is the one it stated at the outset of the hearing: the
Commission should make minimal changes to Schedule LLPS in this case. Tr.
Vol. 6, 50:21-51:1. The evidentiary record supports that position on three
grounds. First, the Commission approved Schedule LLPS less than a year ago,
and the tariff took effect only after this case was filed. Second, Evergy has
billed under the approved tariff and has quoted prospective customers making
siting and expansion decisions under it. Third, no LLPS customer was on
Evergy’s system during the test year, so the record lacks the data needed to
justify changes now.
     Velvet’s data center is located in the Evergy Missouri West service
territory, and Velvet is not presently an Evergy Missouri Metro customer.
     Statement of Facts
     A.    Schedule LLPS was approved less than a year ago and took
effect after this case was filed.
     The Commission approved Evergy’s LLPS Rate Plan for both Evergy
Missouri Metro and Evergy Missouri West in Case No. EO-2025-0154 by
Report and Order issued November 13, 2025. Case No. EO-2025-0154, Report
and Order at 28, 46 (Mo. P.S.C. Nov. 13, 2025). The Commission then approved


                                     1
 Evergy’s compliance tariff sheets implementing Schedule LLPS, effective
March 9, 2026. Case No. EO-2025-0154, Order Approving Tariffs at 1-2 (Mo.
P.S.C. Feb. 25, 2026). Staff witness Sarah Lange confirmed that the tariffs
approved in that case did not take effect until after Evergy filed this rate case.
Tr. Vol. 8, 48:21-49:1.
      B.     Evergy bills under the approved tariff and has quoted
prospective customers under it.
      Evergy witnesses Darrin Ives and Brad Lutz were each heavily involved
in developing the LLPS rate plan approved in that case. Tr. Vol. 7, 187:11-14,
196:14-17.
      Evergy’s testimony is that its current LLPS billing practice complies
with the approved tariff. Tr. Vol. 7, 188:19-22, 197:15-18. Mr. Ives testified that
Evergy has already billed customers under Schedule LLPS using that method
and had not issued any bill under a different method. Tr. Vol. 7, 188:23-189:10.
Mr. Lutz likewise testified that Evergy calculates the minimum monthly bill
according to the terms of Schedule LLPS. Tr. Vol. 7, 197:10-14.
      Mr. Ives also confirmed that when Evergy provided prospective
customers with estimates for siting or expansion decisions, it used the
approved Schedule LLPS method to prepare those projections. Tr. Vol. 7,
189:24-190:4.
      C.     No LLPS customer was in the test year.
      No LLPS customer took service on Evergy Metro’s system during the test
year. Public Counsel’s witness Ron Nelson agreed with that point. Tr. Vol. 7,
177:6-9. Mr. Lutz described this as “a transitional case where we do not have
a customer present in the test year to inform rate making.” Tr. Vol. 12, 114:14-
18. As of the hearing, Evergy had a single Schedule LLPS customer ramping
up service. Tr. Vol. 7, 218:25-219:4.


                                        2
       D.    The proposals before the Commission.
      Public Counsel proposes to raise the LLPS minimum bill requirement
from 80 percent to 90 percent, extend the contract term from 12 to 20 years,
lower the applicability threshold from 75 megawatts to 25 megawatts, and add
a voluntary community benefits rider. Staff proposes several tariff
“clarifications,” including to the ramp period, the definition of contract
demand, and the minimum bill calculation, along with additional reporting
requirements.
      Evergy and Google filed an LLPS Stipulation that, among other things,
changes how billing demand is determined for the LLPS minimum monthly
bill. Staff, Public Counsel and MECG objected, so the LLPS Stipulation is a
joint position of its signatories and the issues it covers remain for the
Commission to decide on the evidence.
      Argument
      I.    Issues 3.A, 3.A.i, 31.A, and 31.B: The Commission should
make minimal changes to Schedule LLPS in this case.
      Senate Bill 4, codified at § 393.130.7, RSMo, requires large electrical
corporations to develop and submit to the Commission large-load schedules
that should reasonably ensure those customers’ rates reflect their
representative share of the costs incurred to serve them and prevent other
customer classes’ rates from reflecting any unjust or unreasonable costs arising
from service to large loads. The Commission applied that mandate less than a
year ago when it approved Schedule LLPS in Case No. EO-2025-0154, finding
that Evergy’s LLPS Rate Plan, as amended by the Agreement, satisfies §
393.130.7. Case No. EO-2025-0154, Report and Order at 28. The evidence in
this case does not support departing from that framework.




                                        3
       A.     The approved tariff already does what Senate Bill 4
requires.
      In Mr. Lutz’s opinion, the tariff approved in Case No. EO-2025-0154
ensures large-load rates reflect those customers’ representative share of the
costs to serve them, and prevents other classes’ rates from reflecting unjust or
unreasonable costs arising from service to large loads. Tr. Vol. 7, 196:25-197:9.
Mr. Ives agreed that the tariff as approved in that case complies with Senate
Bill 4. Tr. Vol. 7, 187:19-22.
      Dr. Geoff Marke agreed that Senate Bill 4 contains consumer protections
and that additional protections are embedded within the approved LLPS tariff,
including minimum bills, minimum demand, financial security, and a distinct
customer class. Tr. Vol. 7, 215:18-216:1, 219:10-18. Nothing in the record shows
that the protections the Commission approved are not working.
      B.     Public Counsel largely re-urges proposals the Commission
considered less than a year ago.
      Dr. Marke testified that his concerns about the LLPS tariff are
“effectively the same concerns” he raised in Case No. EO-2025-0154. Tr. Vol.
7,   216:15-22.   He    agreed   that   his   recommendations      here   repeat
recommendations the Commission rejected in that case, including the
reporting studies and a lower applicability threshold. Tr. Vol. 7, 216:23-218:24.
      Public Counsel’s proposals would also alter what Chair Hahn described
as the “fundamental components” of the tariff: the contract term, the
minimum-demand percentage, and the size threshold. Tr. Vol. 7, 222:23-
224:15. When asked whether any utility or state had adopted all three changes,
Dr. Marke identified none. Id.
      When the Commission approved Schedule LLPS, it recognized the
importance of predictable large-load rates. In rejecting Staff’s alternative in


                                        4
 that case, the Commission found that Staff’s proposal “creates rate instability
for large load customers,” and that under it, “neither a prospective large load
customer nor Evergy on the customer’s behalf could confidently model the
expected rate to inform their site selection efforts, which could drive away large
load customers from the state and deprive ratepayers of the advantages such
customers can provide.” Case No. EO-2025-0154, Report and Order at 18 ¶ 46,
28. That reasoning applies with equal force to substantial changes to the tariff,
or to its interpretation, less than a year after approval.
      C.    Customers and prospective customers have relied on the
tariff as approved.
      A large-load tariff exists to give customers a stable, known set of terms
against which to make long-horizon decisions: where to site a facility, how
much capital to commit, how to plan for power supply, and when to sign a
service agreement. The record shows that reliance has already occurred.
Evergy has billed under the approved tariff, Tr. Vol. 7, 188:19-189:10, 197:10-
18, and Evergy used the approved method to prepare projections for
prospective customers making siting and expansion decisions, Tr. Vol. 7,
189:24-190:4. Those customers made their decisions on the terms this
Commission approved.
      The record also shows how consequential changes can be. The billing-
demand change in the LLPS Stipulation, which its signatories characterize as
a clarification, would increase ramp-period bills. Tr. Vol. 7, 190:8-16, 198:1-6.
Mr. Lutz agreed that, depending on where a customer is in its ramp, the effect
could reach millions of dollars a year. Tr. Vol. 7, 198:7-12. If a single change of
that kind carries that magnitude, the broader changes Staff and Public
Counsel propose would disrupt the expectations on which customers and
prospective customers have already acted.


                                        5
       D.    The record lacks the data needed to support significant
changes.
      No LLPS customer was in the test year. Tr. Vol. 7, 177:6-9; Tr. Vol. 12,
114:14-18. The record therefore contains no representative operating history
for the LLPS class.
      The parties seeking change acknowledged as much. Public Counsel’s Mr.
Nelson agreed that his revenue proposal is an estimate based on forecasts of
future revenues, that no actual recorded revenue of that magnitude exists, and
that his proposal would require the Commission to set rates based on revenues
that have not yet occurred. Tr. Vol. 7, 176:22-178:4. Evergy’s Mr. Lutz
explained that, absent a customer in the test year, the appropriate course is to
hold to the framework approved in Case No. EO-2025-0154 “until we have a
customer available to inform any other behavior that might be different.” Tr.
Vol. 12, 114:14-25.
      Changes of the kind Staff and Public Counsel propose should rest on the
type of evidence the Commission has historically relied on, including actual
LLPS data in a test year. That evidence will exist in a future rate case. It does
not exist in this one.
      Conclusion
      Schedule LLPS was approved recently, customers and prospective
customers have begun relying on it as approved, and this record lacks the data
needed to support significant changes. Velvet respectfully requests that the
Commission refrain from making any significant changes to Schedule LLPS
and maintain the approved framework until a future rate case in which LLPS
operating data is in the test year.




                                       6
                                     Respectfully submitted,

                              By:   /s/ Stephanie S. Bell
                                    Stephanie S. Bell, #61855
                                    Ellinger Bell LLC
                                    308 East High Street, Suite 300
                                    Jefferson City, MO 65101
                                    Telephone: 573-750-4100
                                    Facsimile: 314-334-0450
                                    Email: sbell@ellingerlaw.com

                                    Attorney for Velvet Tech Services, LLC




                       CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

     I hereby certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing was served
upon all of the parties of record or their counsel, pursuant to the Service List
maintained by the Data Center of the Missouri Public Service Commission, on
November 6, 2026.
                                            /s/ Stephanie S. Bell
                                            Stephanie S. Bell
